claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 can be prepared in a homogeneous high-temperature BCC state.
Phase stability in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is governed by competition between the BCC–FCC free-energy difference and a kinetic barrier to atomic diffusion.
The BCC–FCC free-energy difference in this alloy is affected by its Al content.
Approximately 1350–1100 °C is the critical temperature window for the BCC-to-FCC transformation.
Sufficient residence time in the critical temperature range allows the kinetic barrier to be overcome and permits BCC-to-FCC transformation.
Rapid cooling retains metastable BCC at low temperature by suppressing transformation.
Residence time in the 1350–1100 °C range should be varied while composition and prior processing are held constant.
Local atomic configurations and diffusion rates mediate the extent of BCC-to-FCC transformation.
Al-induced free-energy shifts produce a negative free-energy difference that favors FCC over BCC.
Residence at intermediate temperature enables atomic rearrangements needed to nucleate and grow FCC regions.
Slower cooling through 1350–1100 °C will produce a higher FCC phase fraction than rapid cooling.
A rapidly cooled baseline sample will undergo negligible BCC-to-FCC transformation despite a thermodynamic drive toward FCC.
The proposed mechanism is restricted to material having no additional phases or inhomogeneities before cooling.
Diffusion is the rate-limiting process within the stated transformation regime.
Factors other than the proposed diffusion-limited mechanism may dominate far above or below 1350–1100 °C.
Thermodynamic simulations can estimate composition- and temperature-dependent phase stability or free-energy differences in Al-containing high-entropy alloys.
The activation energies for diffusion and nucleation in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 are not precisely known.
Failure of FCC fraction to increase significantly with residence time in 1350–1100 °C would falsify the proposed residence-time mechanism.
Failure of FCC phase fraction to correlate with the predicted free-energy difference would falsify the proposed thermodynamic component of the mechanism.
